Dear Dilnaz,

Thank you for agreeing to mentor me. I had planned to become a topper overnight: every subject, every day. After my result I wrote a list of all my weak points and it was so long I felt sick. You said, "Pick one." So the plan is chemistry only: forty-five minutes on Tuesdays and Thursdays and one longer session on Sunday, with you checking my worked answers on Sunday evening. Everything else stays as it is for now. On Sunday I took the first quiz: 14 out of 20, up from 6. It's small, but I sat there grinning for a full minute. I'm going to keep going.

Mohit

You want to know how I passed chemistry, Gopika? Not the way you'd think.

I'm Reena. After I failed it in Class 11, everybody had big plans for me. My uncle said, "Now you'll top the class." My mother printed a timetable for all six subjects. I tried it for three days and wanted to cry.

Then my mentor at the tuition centre, Mrs. Das, said something different. "Forget topping. Let's just clear chemistry first."

So we made a weekly plan only for chemistry. One chapter a week. Ten questions every evening. A small test every Saturday with her.

The first Saturday I got 12 out of 25. Then 15. Then 19. Honestly, getting 19 felt better than any topper fantasy. It made me believe I could do it.

When I cleared the re-test in October, I started adding physics. One subject at a time.

qa.q: How many questions did Reena do every evening?
How did Reena feel about the six-subject timetable?
qa.a: Reena felt overwhelmed and close to tears after only three days of trying it.

qa.q: What made the smaller target work better than the big plan?
qa.a: Clearing one subject gave Reena quick, visible progress, like 12 then 15 then 19, which built belief and momentum for the rest.

qa.q: How might Mrs. Das have seen the Saturday tests?
qa.a: Mrs. Das likely felt encouraged and pleased, watching the scores rise and knowing the small target was restoring Reena's confidence.

grounding: A spoken account of a student aiming first to clear the weakest subject with a weekly plan and a mentor, using the early success to rebuild momentum.

I'm Mridul, and Divyansh and I share a bench. When he failed maths in the half-yearly, his father pinned a huge chart in his room: eight hours of study daily, all subjects, and "TARGET: 95%" in red. I saw it when I went over for cricket.

For a week Divyansh looked like a ghost. Then something changed. He started staying after school with Mr. Fernandes, the maths teacher, on Tuesdays and Fridays. The big chart came down. A small one went up: just maths, just one chapter a week.

In the class test after a month, he got 18 out of 40. Not great. But he punched the air in the corridor like he'd won a match.

By the next month, he'd added science to the small chart.

I don't know how scared he'd been. But he walked differently after that first 18.

qa.q: How many days a week did Divyansh stay after school with Mr. Fernandes?
qa.a: On Tuesdays and Fridays, twice a week.

qa.q: What might Divyansh have been feeling when he punched the air after scoring 18?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and relieved, since even a modest pass showed him he could make progress.

qa.q: What might happen if Divyansh adds subjects too fast?
qa.a: He could slip back into feeling overwhelmed, so adding one subject at a time, as he did with science, keeps the momentum.

qa.q: How did Divyansh's recovery look to Mridul?
qa.a: To Mridul it looked like a turn from a ghost-like week to someone walking differently, though Mridul cannot know how scared he had been.

grounding: An observer describes a classmate who drops a huge topper plan, works on the weakest subject first with a teacher, and uses an early pass to restart.
